claims.text: The encryption core processes 64-bit blocks using a 256-bit key and 32 rounds. Its round transformation combines addition modulo 2^32, eight 4-bit substitutions, an 11-bit cyclic rotation and XOR.
The 1989 standard leaves substitution tables to a parameter set; RFC 4357 supplies named parameter sets and identifiers.

claims.text: RFC 4357 gives concrete encryption parameter-set encodings and S-box tables.
The reference standard is dated 1989; the preserved English RFC was published in March 2010.
The label GOST 28147-89 is insufficient for interoperable encryption: the S-box parameter set and mode must also be specified.

claims.text: Magma uses a 64-bit block and 256-bit key; its specified encryption composition uses 32 round keys.
Relative to GOST 28147-89, the RFC fixes the S-box set and changes key/block parsing conventions, including big-endian key parsing.
Its national-standard edition is 2015; RFC 8891 was published in September 2020.

claims.text: Replacing a legacy GOST implementation by changing its displayed algorithm name is insufficient: representation and parameter choices can change ciphertext.
The standard specifies a 128-bit block and 256-bit key. Ten round keys are derived, and encryption applies nine keyed substitution/linear-transform layers followed by a final key XOR.
Its nonlinear byte substitution, linear transformation and key schedule are explicitly specified with worked examples.
The Russian standard is the 2015 edition; the English RFC dates to March 2016.
The published transformations and vectors permit independent implementations; implementation agreement can be checked without knowing unpublished round details.
GOST R 34.11-2012 defines 256-bit and 512-bit digest variants. Both use a 512-bit chaining state and specified S, P and L transformations.
The compression function combines a keyed internal transformation with the previous chaining value and message block by XOR; finalization also processes message length and a block sum.
The standard edition is 2012; the preserved English publication is RFC 6986 of August 2013.
A 256-bit digest is an output length. It is not a 256-bit encryption key, and a hash interface does not provide a decryption operation.
The standard defines signing and verification using an elliptic-curve point group over a prime finite field. It specifies signature encodings of 512 or 1024 bits.
The signing rule uses an ephemeral scalar k, point C=kP, r=x_C mod q, and s=(r*d+k*e) mod q, with the specified hash-to-integer and retry rules.
The standard edition is 2012 and the English RFC is dated December 2013.
GOST can name an ecosystem containing signatures, hashes and ciphers. A signature length alone cannot identify the block cipher used by a product.
The examined M-125 machines have ten 30-contact rotors; adjacent rotors move in opposite directions. A punched card sets internal connections, and the machine prints and punches paper tape.

claims.text: The published transformation uses four 32-bit state words, 32 rounds, byte S-box substitution and a linear layer built from XOR and rotations. Both block and key are 128 bits.
In compact notation, the update is X[i+4]=X[i] XOR T(X[i+1] XOR X[i+2] XOR X[i+3] XOR rk[i]); output reverses the final four words.
Diffie and Ledin's dated May 2008 translation reports that SMS4 was issued in January 2006. OSCCA explicitly identified SM4 as formerly SMS4 in its March 2012 announcement.
The official national record gives GB/T 32907-2016 an issue date of 29 August 2016 and an implementation date of 1 March 2017.
A protocol entry such as SM4-GCM identifies a block cipher plus a mode. Its authentication and nonce rules belong to the full protocol profile, rather than to the SM4 round function alone.
SM3 pads messages into 512-bit blocks and updates a 256-bit chaining value with a compression function. That function iterates j from 0 to 63.
The compression state comprises eight 32-bit words, using specified Boolean functions, rotations, additions and permutations P0/P1.
OSCCA announced GM/T 0004-2012 for SM3 on 21 March 2012. RFC 8998 later specifies SM3 in its SM TLS 1.3 profile.
The concrete object is a digest computation, with message expansion and compression, rather than a bulk-encryption key schedule.
The preserved parts separately describe general elliptic-curve operations, signatures, key exchange, public-key encryption and parameter definition.

claims.text: The signature algorithm hashes an identity-bound value with the message; its signing equations include r=(e+x1) mod n and s=(1+d)^(-1)*(k-r*d) mod n, with required retry conditions.
RFC 8998 specifies a 256-bit prime-field curve and uses SM2 signatures with SM3. Its TLS key exchange is ECDHE over that curve.
OSCCA announced the GM/T SM2 family in March 2012. The official GB/T Part 1 record was issued in August 2016 and implemented in March 2017.
Using the SM2 curve for ECDHE in TLS does not by itself mean that the native SM2 Part 3 key-exchange protocol is being executed.

claims.text: Version 1.6 takes a 128-bit key and 128-bit IV and produces 32-bit keystream words. The design combines a 16-cell, 31-bit LFSR, bit reorganization and a nonlinear function.
The preserved specification is dated 28 June 2011 and identifies ZUC as the core for 128-EEA3 and 128-EIA3.
OSCCA included the Zu Chongzhi industry standard in its 21 March 2012 announcement.
The keystream generator, the confidentiality algorithm and the integrity algorithm occupy different interfaces; the name ZUC alone does not specify the full mobile packet-protection procedure.
Turing describes 26-contact rotors, paired reflector contacts, turnover mechanics and plugboard changes. At a fixed machine position, encryption is reciprocal and no letter maps to itself.
The 1940 naval manual records a contemporary operational procedure; it is a separate kind of evidence from a patent or a later cryptanalytic account.
Scherbius's patent record distinguishes its 23 February 1918 application/priority date from publication on 8 July 1925.
Writing the fixed-position wiring as E=T^(-1)*R*T shows why E is its own inverse when the reflector R is an involution. A reflector without fixed points also makes E fixed-point-free.
claims.assumption: T includes all forward wiring and the reflector pairs distinct contacts; composition is evaluated at one fixed stepping state.

claims.text: The wartime dictionary describes five regularly moving chi wheels, five psi wheels with controlled movement, and motor-wheel control of the psi movement.

claims.text: The Newmanry report describes machine-based setting work beginning in December 1942 and pilot Robinson and Tunny machines arriving in April 1943.
The report treats five-impulse teleprinter characters, chi/psi components and addition modulo 2 in its account of Tunny and decoding machines.
At the additive interface C=P XOR K, reuse of the same keystream yields C1 XOR C2=P1 XOR P2. This is a property of keystream reuse, independent of the number of wheels.
claims.assumption: The two messages use the same keystream at aligned bit positions.

claims.text: BSI dates the Windows Chiasmus file-encryption program to 2001, followed by a Linux command-line version. Partners had to exchange secret key material beforehand.
BSI describes non-open algorithms and standards and proprietary software; it says Chiasmus key material is incompatible with replacement products.
BSI states that the VS-NfD approval was withdrawn on 30 June 2022. Its SINA history separately records replacing CHIASMUS by AES at lower classification levels.
A file archive or migration tool needs the actual container, key format and implementation behavior; merely selecting another symmetric cipher cannot make a Chiasmus file readable.

BSI's SINA history says development was commissioned from secunet in 1999. It identifies LIBELLE as an HSM-implemented algorithm used at higher classification levels and describes gradual replacement by a newly approved algorithm.

claims.text: Camellia was jointly developed by NTT and Mitsubishi Electric. It has a 128-bit block and 128-, 192- and 256-bit key options.
The data path has 18 rounds for 128-bit keys and 24 rounds for the larger keys, with FL and FLINV functions inserted every six rounds.
The designer archive identifies a 12 July 2000 CRYPTREC specification and a 26 September 2001 version 2.0. The English RFC followed in April 2004.

source_refs.locator: Version 2.0 title and revision record; companion 2000 submission S052

claims.text: A 128-bit block interface with several key sizes does not imply AES internals: Camellia's specified data path is a Feistel construction with additional keyed layers.
Sony's version 1.0 specification is dated 1 June 2007. It uses four 32-bit data branches and 18, 22 or 26 rounds for the three key sizes.
The data-processing part uses a four-branch generalized Feistel network; an eight-branch construction also appears in scheduling larger keys.
The English RFC specification was published in March 2011 and dates the algorithm's public publication to 2007.
The four-branch structure is a concrete design distinction, despite sharing a 128-bit block interface and key-size choices with several other ciphers.
RFC 4269 describes SEED as developed by KISA since 1998 and as a Korean national standard. It specifies a 128-bit block, a 128-bit key and 16 Feistel rounds.
The public round description includes S-box transformations, permutations, XOR and addition, with an explicit key schedule and test data.
The preserved RFC is dated December 2005 and replaces the earlier RFC 4009 description.
SEED provides an example where both the primitive's structure and development period can be stated from a published specification, while product certification remains a separate question.
RFC 5794 dates development by Korean cryptographers to 2003 and Korean standardization to 2004. It specifies 128-bit blocks with 12, 14 or 16 rounds depending on key size.
The round transformations alternate substitution layers, use XOR key addition and a diffusion map A satisfying A(A(x))=x.
The preserved English RFC was published in March 2010.
The diffusion map's involution is a specific algebraic property. It does not mean encryption is self-inverse without the specified key-schedule and round transformations.
